title: Korjauttaa vai korjata?
subtitle: Having something fixed, versus fixing it yourself

blocks.text: Huollattanut and korjauttanut sat side by side, unglossed, in Lesson 23's vocabulary — olen huollattanut, 'I have had [my car] serviced'. There's a whole verb-building pattern behind that extra -tta-, and it's exactly the distinction a car-repair corpus needs: did you do it, or did you have someone else do it for you?

blocks.translation: To have it fixed by someone, or to fix it yourself?

blocks.title: Why every review needs this distinction
blocks.text: A whole review corpus about repair shops is, almost by definition, about causative actions — customers don't fix their own cars, they have shops fix them. This one small verb-building trick is quietly doing enormous work throughout the entire corpus.

blocks.content: To turn a plain verb into 'have [someone] do it', insert {-tta-|grammar|causative infix|have (someone) do} or -ttä- into the stem before the normal ending. Korjata (to fix, yourself) → {korjauttaa|grammar|causative verb|to have (something) fixed}. Huoltaa (to service/maintain) → {huollattaa|grammar|causative verb|to have (something) serviced}.

items.en: I took the car to have it fixed.

items.fi: Olen {huollattanut|grammar|causative verb, past participle|had [my car] serviced} täällä viisi vuotta.
items.en: I have had [my car] serviced here for five years.

blocks.text: Piece 2 — Comparing the plain and causative side by side

blocks.title: One small syllable, a whole different meaning
blocks.text: Korjata means 'to fix' — the subject fixes it themselves. Korjauttaa means 'to have it fixed' — the subject arranges for someone else to do it. Compare korjasin auton (I fixed the car, myself) with korjautin auton (I had the car fixed, by a shop) — both perfectly grammatical, describing very different levels of hands-on involvement.

items.fi: {Korjasin|grammar|1st person past, plain verb|I fixed} auton itse.
{Korjautin|grammar|1st person past, causative verb|I had fixed} auton muualla.
items.en: I had the car fixed elsewhere.

blocks.text: Piece 3 — More causatives you'll meet in the corpus

blocks.content: This pattern extends beyond cars: uusia (to renew) → uusittaa; teettää, from tehdä, meaning 'to have [something] made/done'. Once you know to look for -tta-/-ttä- sitting inside a familiar verb, you can decode this whole family yourself.

items.en: I had my car fixed elsewhere for 105 euros.
I would no longer have my car serviced here.

lines.speaker: A
lines.fi: Korjasitko auton itse, vai korjautitko sen jossain?
lines.en: Did you fix the car yourself, or did you have it fixed somewhere?

lines.speaker: B
lines.fi: Korjautin sen muualla. Olen huollattanut autoani siellä viisi vuotta.
lines.en: I had it fixed elsewhere. I've had my car serviced there for five years.

lines.speaker: A
lines.en: Would you have it serviced here going forward?

blocks.title: Paul Noble Rule
blocks.text: Whenever you meet a verb that looks slightly longer than one you already know — an extra -tta-/-ttä- sitting in the middle — check whether it means 'have someone else do X' instead of 'do X'. This single check unlocks huollattanut, korjauttaa, korjautin, and any new causative verb you'll meet from here on.

blocks.content: Korjauttaa: KOR-yaut-taa (four syllables, the extra -tta- makes it noticeably longer than korjata). Huollattaa: HUOL-lat-taa (the 'uo' glides, double t held). Korjautin: KOR-yau-tin (three syllables, past tense 'I' ending -n at the very end).
